cards.explanation: The answer is that they forsake the Law of the LORD. After Rehoboam had established his sovereignty and royal power, he and all Israel with him forsook the Law of the LORD (2 Chronicles 12:1). The power was in place, and the Law still got left behind. I think that's the sneaky part, friends: it happened after his rule was established.

The answer is Egypt. Shishak is king of Egypt, and he attacks Jerusalem in Rehoboam's fifth year because they had been unfaithful to the LORD (2 Chronicles 12:2). So this army came marching up from Egypt. That's a LONG walk with chariots.

The answer is True. Shishak, king of Egypt, captured the fortified cities of Judah and came as far as Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 12:4). Those were the very kind of cities Rehoboam had built up earlier (2 Chronicles 11:5). Walls are great, friends, but they didn't stop this army.

The answer is that the LORD says, because they left Him, He has handed them over to Shishak. Shemaiah the prophet tells them, “This is what the LORD says: ‘You have forsaken Me; therefore, I have forsaken you into the hand of Shishak.’…” (2 Chronicles 12:5) It's a hard word to hear. But the LORD tells them plainly what's going on.
The answer is humble. The leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” (2 Chronicles 12:6) I tell you, friends, I think saying that out loud takes some guts.

The answer is False. The king and the leaders humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” (2 Chronicles 12:6) Saying He is righteous is the opposite of calling Him unfair. I think that's a good sign they heard Him.

The answer is that He will not destroy them. When the LORD saw that they had humbled themselves, He told Shemaiah, “They have humbled themselves; I will not destroy them, but will soon grant them deliverance.” (2 Chronicles 12:7) The word from the LORD came after they humbled themselves. Humbling themselves matters.

The answer is to learn the difference between serving Him and serving other kings. They will become Shishak's servants, “…so that they may learn the difference between serving Me and serving the kings of other lands.” (2 Chronicles 12:8) So being spared from destruction doesn't mean everything goes back to normal. They're going to find out what serving other kings is like. I bet that's a lesson they remember.

The answer is bronze. After Shishak took the gold shields Solomon had made, King Rehoboam made bronze shields in their place (2 Chronicles 12:9-10). Solomon was David's son and Israel's king (1 Kings 2:12). The gold's gone, but the guards still have shields in their hands.

The answer is True. Whenever the king entered the house of the LORD, the guards would go with him, bearing the shields, and later they would return them to the guardroom (2 Chronicles 12:11). Those bronze shields had a whole routine. Out with the king, then back to the guardroom.

The answer is that the anger turns away from him. Because Rehoboam humbled himself, the anger of the LORD turned away from him, and He did not destroy him completely (2 Chronicles 12:12). Humbling himself made a real difference. I love that, friends.

The answer is good. The LORD did not destroy Rehoboam completely, and the text says, “Indeed, conditions were good in Judah.” (2 Chronicles 12:12) After an army, lost treasure and bronze shields, that's a pretty nice turnaround. Humbling yourself pays off.

The answer is that he did not set his heart to seek the LORD. That's the reason the writer gives: “And Rehoboam did evil because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.” (2 Chronicles 12:14) The reason is about the heart, not about armies or allies. I think that's worth sitting with, friends.

The answer is False. “There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their days.” (2 Chronicles 12:15) Jeroboam was the king of Israel (1 Kings 12:20). So even with conditions good in Judah (2 Chronicles 12:12), the writer still records war between them.

The answer is Abijah. When Rehoboam rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David, his son Abijah reigned in his place (2 Chronicles 12:16). Rehoboam had other sons too (2 Chronicles 11:18-20). This one took the throne. The story of Rehoboam's reign ends here.
